title: Ill Winds 1
content:
"Aaaaaaagh—!!!"

Wang Lingjiao bolted upright in bed, shrieking her lungs out. At the table across the room, Wen Chao slammed his palm down so hard the teacups rattled. "What the hell are you screaming for in the middle of the night?!"

Gasping for breath, her chest heaving, she stammered, "I... I dreamed of that Wei guy again. It's him, it's always him!"

"I chucked him down the Burial Mounds over three months ago!" Wen Chao snapped. "How the hell are you still having nightmares about him? How many times is this now?!"

"I... I don't know! He just won't leave my head lately!"

Wen Chao was already beside himself with fury over the war reports in front of him. He had zero patience left for her, and certainly no desire to play the doting lover and tuck her back in. He sneered, "Then don't go to sleep!"

Scrambling out of bed, she threw herself against his desk. "Wen-gongzi, I... the more I think about it, the more terrified I get. Did we... did we make a massive mistake back then? What if he didn't die down there? What if he..."

A thick vein throbbed violently at Wen Chao’s temple. "Are you insane? How many strike teams did my father send into those Burial Mounds over the years? Did a single one ever make it back? That brat was tossed into the deepest pit; by now, his corpse has probably rotted through two rounds of maggots."

"Even if he’s dead, it's still terrifying!" she wailed. "What if he actually did what he swore he'd do? What if he turned into a fierce wraith and crawled back for us—"

The words hung in the air, and for a fleeting, suffocating second, both of them vividly recalled the look on Wei Ying’s face as he plummeted into the dark that day. That expression. A cold shudder ran down their spines in unison.

Wen Chao scrambled to break the chill, his voice rising defensive and harsh. "Bullshit! Even dead, he's trapped! Every soul that perishes in the Burial Mounds is shackled there for eternity. Stop scaring yourself with ghost stories! Can't you see I've got enough on my mind?!"

He crumpled the military dispatch in his fist, hurling it across the floor with a venomous curse. "What a joke—the Sunshot Campaign?! Shooting down the sun? They're living in a goddamn dream world!"

Wang Lingjiao pushed herself up and carefully poured him a cup of warm tea. Brain working fast, she smoothed her expression into a syrupy, flirtatious pout. "Wen-gongzi, those upstarts won't be riding high for long. Wen-zongzhu will crush them in no time, and then—"

"Shut your mouth!" Wen Chao spat. "You don't know a damn thing! Get out. Don't test my patience!"

Swallowing a mix of humiliation and spite, Wang Lingjiao set the cup down. She smoothed her hair, adjusted her sheer robes, pasted on a sweet smile, and slipped out the door.

The moment the door clicked shut behind her, the smile melted off her face.

She opened her palm to reveal the crumpled ball of parchment she’d discreetly snatched off the floor on her way out. She had to know what had made him lose his temper like that. Her literacy was patchy at best, but after squinting and puzzling over the characters for several agonizing minutes, the blood drained straight from her cheeks.

Wen Xu, the clan leader’s eldest son and Wen Chao’s older brother, had been beheaded in battle by one of the rebel leaders. His severed head was currently impaled on a pike, paraded before the allied frontline.

Wang Lingjiao stood frozen.

First, Gusu Lan had been burned. Then Yunmeng Jiang had been slaughtered. Countless smaller sects had been trampled underfoot. People had grumbled, sure, but Qishan Wen had always stamped out resistance before it could even spark. So when the Jin, Nie, Lan, and Jiang clans joined forces three months ago, raising the banner of the Sunshot Campaign, no one on their side had taken it seriously.

Even Wen-zongzhu had scoffed at the time. The Lanling Jin Clan were spineless fence-sitters—jumping on the righteous bandwagon now, but the second the battle turned sour, they’d come crawling back on their knees, crying for mercy. The leader of Qinghe Nie was too rigid for his own good; men like that snapped easily, bound to die at the hands of their own subordinates sooner or later. Gusu Lan was already broken; Lan Xichen had salvaged a few crates from their library to play acting clan leader, but he was just a kid out of his depth. And Yunmeng Jiang was the biggest joke of all—their sect was wiped off the map, leaving behind Jiang Cheng, an arrogant brat even younger than Lan Xichen. With no army to his name, he actually had the audacity to call himself a clan leader, waging a war while desperately recruiting strays on the fly.

Eight words had summed up the Wen Clan’s verdict: Powerless runts, wildly punching above their weight.

Everyone backed by the Wen Clan had treated the Sunshot Campaign like a bad comedy. But three months in, the script had flipped on its head.

Losing key strategic outposts like Hejian and Yunmeng was one thing. But now... even the clan leader’s eldest son had been decapitated.

Trembling with a sickening dread, Wang Lingjiao crept down the silent corridor and ducked into her own chambers. Her left eyelid wouldn't stop twitching. Pressing a hand over her eye and clutching her chest, her mind raced, hunting for an exit strategy.

She’d been at Wen Chao’s side for nearly six months. In Wen Chao’s world, six months was the absolute expiration date for his infatuation with any woman. She had genuinely believed she was special—that she’d be the one who stuck around. But his mounting irritability and open disgust over the past few weeks had made one thing painfully clear: she was just another piece of meat to him.

Gnawing on her lower lip, she dropped to her knees and dragged a small wooden chest out from beneath the bed.

Inside were the treasures, talismans, and gold she’d spent the last six months shamelessly skimming off Wen Chao. The gold would buy her a new life; the spiritual tools would keep her breathing. Bitter as it was to cut her losses, the writing was on the wall.

Fumbling for the tiny brass key tucked into her sash, she jammed it into the lock, muttering under her breath, "Greasy toad bastard... you're going to get your throat cut anyway. Good riddance, you think I actually enjoyed serving you—ah!"

She scrambled backward on her elbows, a strangled shriek tearing from her throat.

For a split second, as the lid creaked open, she had seen what was inside.

No gold. No jewelry.

Just a pale, bloodless child, curled tightly into a ball inside the dark chest.

Panting in sheer terror, she kicked her legs out, scuttling backward across the floorboards. The chest was always locked! She kept the only key on her person day and night! How could a child be in there?! She barely opened it once a month—if a kid had been stuffed inside, how could she have missed it? How could it even be alive?!

Her flailing feet had knocked the chest over. It lay face down on the floor, perfectly still.

Trembling from head to toe, she forced herself up. She wanted to creep forward and look, but terror nailed her boots to the ground. A ghost... there’s a ghost in here!

Her own cultivation was practically nonexistent; if an actual spirit was haunting her, she stood zero chance. But then it hit her: this was a Supervisory Office! High-grade warding talismans were plastered across every doorframe and outer gate. If something foul was lurking around, those charms would keep her safe.

She bolted into the hallway, ripped the protective yellow paper right off her door, and slapped it straight over her chest.

With the talisman pressed over her racing heart, a fragile wave of relief washed through her. Armed with a long wooden laundry pole, she crept back inside and used the tip to flip the chest right-side up from a safe distance.

Her jewelry and gold sat stacked in neat, gleaming rows. No child. Nothing.

Exhaling a long, shaky breath, she lowered the pole and crouched down, reaching out to count her stash.

Out of the corner of her eye, two pinpricks of white light caught her attention beneath the bed.

A pair of eyes.

A pale, translucent child was lying flat on its stomach in the shadows under the frame, staring right back at her.

In his study, Wen Chao’s ears rang with Wang Lingjiao’s piercing shriek for the third time that night. His rage boiled over.

"Useless bitch!" he roared, kicking a stool across the room. "Jumping at shadows all damn night—can't I catch a single second of peace?!"

If not for the endless stream of disastrous war dispatches giving him migraines, leaving him no time to scout new women—and if he weren't paranoid that a new concubine might be an assassin planted by the rebel clans—he would’ve tossed her out on the street weeks ago. He barked toward the hall, "Guard! Go shut her up!"

Silence.

He sent another chair crashing into the wall. "Where the hell is everyone?!"

With a sharp creak, the double doors swung wide.

"I told you to shut that woman up, not barge into my—"

The rest of the sentence died in his throat.

A woman was standing in the doorway.

Her face was an abomination. It looked as though her skull had been shattered into pieces and sloppily glued back together. Her eyes stared in completely different directions—the left rolled toward the ceiling, the right fixed on the floorboards. Her features were twisted into a grotesque, horrifying mask.

It took Wen Chao several agonizing seconds, piecing together the familiar cut of her revealing silk robes, to recognize who it was.

Wang Lingjiao!

A wet, gurgling sound scraped from her throat. She took a dragging step toward him, raising a trembling hand. "...Save... save me... help me..."

Wen Chao lost his mind. Drawing his new sword, he slashed wildly at her. "Get away from me! Get back!"

The blade bit deep into her shoulder, wrenching her contorted face into an even more gruesome grimace as she shrieked, "Aaaaaagh! It hurts—it hurts so bad—!"

Terrified to even yank the steel free, Wen Chao grabbed a wooden stool and hurled it with all his might. The heavy timber shattered across her chest. She swayed, her knees giving out, and she collapsed to the floorboards, bowing frantically as if kowtowing to an invisible figure.

"...I'm sorry... I'm sorry... please spare me, spare me, spare me..."

With every violent strike of her forehead against the wood, dark blood poured from her eyes, nose, ears, and mouth.

She was blocking the doorway; running that way was out of the question. Wen Chao lunged for the window, shoving the shutters wide and screaming at the top of his lungs: "Wen Zhuliu! Wen Zhuliu—!!!"

On the floor behind him, Wang Lingjiao had picked up a broken stool leg. Laughing hysterically through her tears, she began violently jamming the blunt wood down her own throat.

"Okay, okay! I'll eat it, I'll eat! Haha, I'll eat it all!"

She was actually forcing the thick timber down her gullet, inch by agonizing inch!

His soul practically leaving his body, Wen Chao vaulted onto the sill, preparing to jump.

Then he froze.

Down in the courtyard, drenched in cold, pristine moonlight, stood a solitary figure in black.

Around the same time.

Jiang Cheng stood at the edge of a dense forest. Hearing approaching footsteps, he glanced sideways.

A figure in immaculate white robes stepped through the trees, a forehead ribbon fluttering gently in the night breeze, his pale features carved like jade under the moon, radiating an ethereal, frosty elegance.

Jiang Cheng greeted him coldly. "Lan-er-gongzi."

Lan Wangji’s expression was solemn as he dipped his chin. "Jiang-zongzhu."

Neither man was one for small talk. Nodding in mutual acknowledgment, they signaled their respective disciples and took to their swords, cutting through the night sky in stony silence.

Two months ago, the Twin Jades of Lan and Jiang Cheng had launched a daring raid on Wen Chao’s "Re-education Office," reclaiming the spiritual blades confiscated from the clan heirs. That was how Sandu and Bichen had finally found their way back to their masters' sides.

Lan Wangji’s pale gaze flicked down toward the second sword resting at Jiang Cheng’s waist before returning to the path ahead.

After a long silence, he asked evenly, "Still no word of Wei Ying?"

Jiang Cheng glanced at him, clearly surprised by the sudden question. "None."

His fingers brushed against the hilt of Suibian. "My scouts haven't turned up a single lead. But the moment he comes back, he'll seek me out. When he does, I'll hand his blade back to him."

Before long, their joint force reached the outskirts of the Supervisory Office where Wen Chao was holed up, preparing for a midnight raid. But before they could breach the gates, Lan Wangji’s gaze sharpened, and Jiang Cheng’s brow furrowed deep.

Resentful energy was bleeding into the night, heavy, suffocating, and thick as oil.

Yet the warding charms lining the outer gates remained completely intact. Jiang Cheng flashed a hand sign; his disciples fanned out, melting into the shadows along the perimeter wall. With a sharp flick of his wrist, a streak of purple sword-glare burst from Sandu, blasting the heavy gates off their hinges.

Before stepping across the threshold, Lan Wangji’s eyes lingered on the talismans flanking the entrance.

Inside, the courtyard was a slaughterhouse.

Corpses carpeted the flagstones. Not just the yard—bodies were tangled in the flower beds, draped over the verandas, slumped across balustrades, and even impaled along the tiled rooftops.

Every single body wore the sunburst robes of Qishan Wen.

Jiang Cheng used the tip of Sandu to flip a corpse over. The man's pale face was streaked with crusted lines of black blood. "Bled out from all seven orifices."

Lan Wangji called from a few paces away, "Not this one."

Jiang Cheng strode over. The corpse before Lan Wangji had its eyes rolled back into its skull, facial muscles frozen in a horrific grimace, a pool of yellow bile pooled around its lips. Scared to death. Literally.

A Jiang disciple jogged up, reporting grimly, "Sect Leader, we've swept the grounds. Everyone is dead. But... every single body died a different death."

Strangled, burned alive, drowned, poisoned, frozen to the bone, throats torn open, skulls caved in...

Jiang Cheng’s voice dropped to a chilling whisper. "Looks like someone beat us to the punch tonight."

Without a word, Lan Wangji was the first to cross into the master quarters.

The doors to Wen Chao’s bedchamber hung wide open, housing only a single female corpse. She was dressed in sheer, disheveled silks, a wooden stool leg shoved deep into her mouth. She had literally choked herself to death trying to force the solid timber down her own throat.

Jiang Cheng flipped her twisted face toward the light. Staring down at her, a cold sneer broke across his lips. Grabbing the exposed end of the wood, he shoved it forward with savage force, driving the remaining half straight down her gullet.

His eyes burned red as he pushed himself upright, about to speak, when he noticed Lan Wangji standing rigid by the doorframe, deep in thought. He walked over, tracking Lan Wangji’s gaze to a yellow talisman inked in cinnabar, plastered against the wood.

At a glance, it looked like a standard ward. But a closer inspection revealed subtle, deeply unsettling strokes.

Lan Wangji murmured, "Extra strokes."

Jiang Cheng’s eyes narrowed. "You're right."

Every disciple of a prominent clan had the stroke order of standard household wards drilled into their bones by the age of fifteen. Yet hidden within the sweeping cinnabar lines of this charm were several extra slashes. And those few deliberate brushstrokes completely perverted the talisman's entire structural flow. Looked at from the right angle, the red ink resembled a human face grinning back with a hideous, mocking sneer.

A thorough sweep of the outpost yielded no sign of Wen Chao or Wen Zhuliu. Guessing they were fleeing back toward Qishan, Jiang Cheng immediately pulled his men out to pursue them on sword. Lan Wangji, however, took a brief detour back to Gusu.

It wasn't until the following evening that Lan Wangji caught up with the vanguard. Producing the altered talisman from his sleeve, he said flatly, "This charm was inverted."

Jiang Cheng frowned. "Inverted? What do you mean?"

"A standard talisman repels evil spirits," Lan Wangji explained. "This one attracts them."

Jiang Cheng stared in disbelief. "A talisman... that lures dark entities? That's unheard of."

"It is. Yet tests confirm it draws in malevolent energy like a beacon."

Jiang Cheng took the paper, holding it up to the moonlight. "Just a few extra strokes, and the entire function flips on its head? A person did this?"

"Four strokes were added, drawn in human blood," Lan Wangji murmured. "Every protective charm in that outpost was altered the exact same way. The brushwork belongs to a single hand."

Jiang Cheng’s jaw tightened. "Who could pull off something like that? None of the prominent cultivators I know have that kind of craft." He paused, shaking his head. "Doesn't matter who they are, as long as we're pointing our swords in the same direction: slaughtering Wen dogs!"

Tracking reports of carnage, the pair pushed north. Everywhere they passed, rumors of grotesque, butchered corpses preceded them. Every single victim wore the sunburst robes of Qishan Wen—high-ranking cultivators boasting impressive martial cores. Yet every single one had died in horrific, imaginative agony, their corpses strung up in bustling public squares for the world to see.

Jiang Cheng asked, "You think the same person did all this?"

"The demonic malice runs heavy," Lan Wangji replied quietly. "It is the work of one man."

Jiang Cheng sneered, "Demonic? In this world, is there anything more demonic than a Wen dog?!"

By the dead of night on the fourth day, they finally caught Wen Zhuliu’s trail outside a remote mountain outpost.

The relay station had two floors, flanked by a horse stable. The moment Lan Wangji and Jiang Cheng touched down, they caught sight of a towering silhouette darting inside and bolting the heavy front door from within. Wary of Wen Zhuliu’s lethal Core-Melting Hand, they avoided a frontal breach, leaping soundlessly onto the tiled roof instead. Grinding his teeth so hard his jaw ached, Jiang Cheng peered through a crack in the roof tiles, eyes blazing with venom.

Covered in travel grime, Wen Zhuliu stumbled upstairs with heavy, dragging steps, carrying a bundled figure in his arms. He deposited his charge by the table, rushed to the windows to draw the thick curtains tight, and only then returned to light a small oil lamp.

The dim flame washed over his features—ashen, hollow, and shadowed by dark, bruised rings beneath his eyes. The figure slumped beside him was bundled head to toe in a heavy traveling cloak, trembling violently like a fragile, dying cocoon. A wet, wheezing rasp tore from the fabric: "Don't light the lamp! What if he finds us?!"

Lan Wangji looked up, trading a sharp, bewildered glance with Jiang Cheng.

That had to be Wen Chao. But why was his voice so shrill, cracked, and pathetic? It sounded nothing like him.

Rummaging through his sleeves for medicine, Wen Zhuliu muttered flatly, "Do you honestly think staying in the dark will keep him from tracking you?"

Wen Chao gasped for breath, stammering frantically, "We... we ran so far! We've been running for days! He... he can't possibly catch up now, right?!"

Wen Zhuliu replied with cool indifference, "Perhaps."

Wen Chao snapped, his voice pitching into a panicked shriek: "What the hell does 'perhaps' mean?! If we haven't lost him, why aren't you running?!"

"You need medicine. Otherwise, you won't survive the night."

With a swift yank, Wen Zhuliu pulled the hood back.

The two men on the roof froze.

Beneath the fabric lay neither the arrogant smirk nor the greasy, handsome features of Wen Chao.

What stared back was a bald, bandage-wrapped skull.

As Wen Zhuliu peeled the linen away layer by layer like shedding charred skin, the flesh underneath was exposed to the weak lamplight. The face was an unrecognizable mess of mottled burns and weeping scabs, looking as though it had been boiled alive in oil—a grotesque, hideous ruin stripped of every trace of his former self.

Uncorking a porcelain vial, Wen Zhuliu shoved several medicinal pills past Wen Chao's lips, then scooped a thick salve to smear across the raw burns covering his scalp and face. Wen Chao whimpered in agony, but Wen Zhuliu warned in a monotone drone: "Do not weep. The salt from your tears will fester in the open sores and make it burn worse."

Wen Chao clenched his jaw, choking back the sobs. Beneath the flickering, dying flame of the lamp, a scarred, bald freak bared his teeth, letting out muffled, inhuman groans in the dark. It was a sight of sheer, unadulterated horror.

Suddenly, Wen Chao let out a bloodcurdling scream: "The flute! The flute! Is that the flute?! I hear him playing it again!"

Wen Zhuliu snapped, "It isn't! It's just the wind!"

Yet Wen Chao had already tumbled off his chair in a frantic frenzy, howling as he clawed at the floorboards. Wen Zhuliu had to haul him back up into his seat. It seemed his legs were ruined; he couldn't even stand on his own anymore.

Finishing the bandages, Wen Zhuliu pulled a few cold steamed buns from his robes and pressed them into the man's hands. "Eat. Once you're done, we keep moving."

Trembling, Wen Chao brought a bun to his lips and took a bite.

Watching from the rafters, the memory of his own desperate flight with Wei Wuxian flashed through Jiang Cheng’s mind—starving, hunted, unable to scrounge up a single mouthful of dry bread. Seeing the beast brought this low was pure, unadulterated karma.

A fierce, triumphant grin split Jiang Cheng’s face as he laughed silently in the dark.

Suddenly, Wen Chao’s teeth caught on something. His eyes bulged with pure, hysterical horror as he hurled the bun across the room, screeching: "I'm not eating meat! I won't eat it! I won't! No meat!!!"

Wen Zhuliu handed him another. "This one is vegetable."

Wen Chao swatted it away. "I said no! Get it away from me! Get out! I want my father—when are we getting back to my father?!"

"At our current pace, two days."

Wen Zhuliu spoke with blunt, unvarnished honesty—no exaggerations, no empty promises. Yet that flat reality broke what little sanity Wen Chao had left. He rasped, "Two days?! Two days?! Look at me! Look at what he’s done to me! If I wait another two days, what will be left of me?! You useless piece of trash!"

Wen Zhuliu rose abruptly.

Terrified that his protector was abandoning him, Wen Chao shrank back, panic instantly overriding his temper. His guards had been butchered one by one before his very eyes; this man was his only shield, his final lifeline. He backpedaled frantically: "No, no, no! Wen Zhuliu, Brother Wen! Don't leave! You can't leave me! If you bring me back to my father, I'll make sure he promotes you to the highest-ranking guest elder! No—you saved my life, you're my brother! I'll have him formally adopt you into the main clan! You'll be my older brother from now on!"

Wen Zhuliu’s gaze remained locked on the wooden staircase. "No need."

Not only had he heard it—Lan Wangji and Jiang Cheng had caught the sound too.

From the stairs of the relay station came a slow, rhythmic cadence.

Footsteps.

Step by deliberate step, someone was ascending the stairs.

The remaining color drained from Wen Chao’s scarred, weeping face. Shaking violently, he thrust his hands out from beneath the cloak, pressing his palms over his eyes in a childish, desperate attempt to shut the nightmare out.

And those hands... were smooth, mangled stumps.

Every single finger had been chopped clean off.

Thump. Thump. Thump.

The figure climbed at an unhurried, measured pace. Draped in flowing black robes, tall and lean, a pitch-black flute tucked into his sash, he strolled up the landing with his hands resting casually behind his back.

Up on the roof, Lan Wangji and Jiang Cheng gripped their sword hilts in unison.

The man reached the top of the stairs, turning around with a faint, lazy smile.

Catching sight of that familiar, razor-sharp, handsome face, Lan Wangji’s eyes blew wide in absolute, shattered disbelief.
